Synopsis: In the final film of the Heisei Godzilla series, a meltdown is occurring within Godzilla's nuclear body — his temperature rising inexorably toward total meltdown, which could destroy the planet. Simultaneously, Godzilla Jr., his son, faces a catastrophic new enemy called Destoroyah, a creature created from the original Oxygen Destroyer used to kill the first Godzilla in 1954. The film functions as both a spectacle and a genuine farewell, staging the death of the character Toho had built for forty years with considerable emotional weight.

Title: Memories
Director: Koji Morimoto, Tensai Okamura, Katsuhiro Otomo
Synopsis: An anthology of three animated short films produced by Katsuhiro Otomo. Magnetic Rose (directed by Koji Morimoto) sends two salvagers into a derelict spacecraft where a dead opera singer's obsessions have taken on physical form. Stink Bomb (directed by Tensai Okamura) follows a hapless lab worker who accidentally becomes a biological weapon and can't figure out why everyone is fleeing him. Cannon Fodder (directed by Katsuhiro Otomo) is a sustained single-day portrait of a militarised city whose entire civilization is organised around the operation of a vast cannon that perpetually fires at an unseen enemy.

Title: Salaam Cinema
Synopsis: To mark the centenary of cinema in 1995, Mohsen Makhmalbaf placed a newspaper advertisement inviting anyone who dreamed of becoming an actor to come to an open call. Over a hundred people arrived; the film records the auditions. What Makhmalbaf actually creates is something between a documentary and a performance in itself — as he tests, humiliates, instructs, and breaks down the would-be actors, the boundary between his film's subject (the desire to perform) and his own directorial act of control dissolves into something uncomfortable and revealing about power and the camera.

Title: Shinjuku Boys
Synopsis: A documentary by British filmmakers Kim Longinotto and Jano Williams following three female-to-male transgender individuals — known as onnabes — who work as hosts in a Shinjuku club, entertaining female clientele in the tradition of Tokyo's male host bars. The film respectfully and intimately documents their self-understanding, their relationships both inside and outside the club, and the ways they navigate Japanese society's rigid gender categories while living fully in the identities they have claimed. One of the earliest Western documentary portraits of transgender lives in Japan.

Title: Tales from the Hood
Synopsis: Three young drug dealers arrive at a funeral home run by a bizarre mortician who insists on showing them the bodies in his keep and telling the stories behind each one — each story a horror anthology tale addressing a different facet of racial violence in America: a murdered Black politician haunting the cops who killed him; a Black child beaten at home by his mother's abusive white boyfriend; a racist Southern senator menaced by the spirits of lynching victims; a gang member in psychological rehabilitation. Rusty Cundieff's film uses the horror genre as a vehicle for direct political commentary.

Title: The Celluloid Closet
Synopsis: A documentary tracing the representation — or systematic suppression and distortion of representation — of gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender people in Hollywood cinema from the silent era to the early 1990s. Based on Vito Russo's foundational 1981 book, the film constructs its argument through a vast selection of film clips accompanied by commentary from actors, directors, and writers including Lily Tomlin, Whoopi Goldberg, Tony Curtis, and Gore Vidal, revealing how homosexuality was stereotyped, coded, coded against, and occasionally transcended within the industry's self-policing constraints.

Title: Tokyo Fist
Synopsis: A mild-mannered salaryman named Tsuda runs into Taguchi, a former acquaintance who has become a professional boxer, and the reunion detonates within his previously controlled life — Taguchi steals his fiancée and Tsuda responds not by normative assertion but by beginning to train as a boxer himself, descending into a masochistic physicality that transforms his relationship to his own body. Tsukamoto directs in his characteristic mode of visceral, handheld intensity, and the film becomes an exploration of Japanese masculinity, body horror, and the strange liberation of embracing damage.

Title: Twelve Monkeys
Synopsis: A prisoner named James Cole is sent back from a devastated 2035 — where the survivors of a man-made plague hide underground — to gather information about the virus that wiped out most of humanity and trace its origin to a shadowy organisation called the Army of the Twelve Monkeys. Cole arrives in 1990 and then 1996, diagnosed as delusional by a psychiatrist named Railly, while Brad Pitt plays a frenetic, unpredictable revolutionary whose connection to the plague may be less direct than it seems. Terry Gilliam's time-travel film is one of the most formally sophisticated and emotionally devastating science fiction films of the decade.

Title: Up, Down, Fragile
Synopsis: Three young women in Paris — Ninon, searching for her biological mother; Louise, a nightclub singer; and Marie, recently arrived from the provinces — form connections with each other and with the city over the course of a summer, their paths crossing through a series of encounters that feel both spontaneous and mysteriously fated. Jacques Rivette's late musical is deliberately light and playful, structured around songs and chance with the improvisational freedom and pleasure in performance that defines the best of his work. It is a graceful, autumnal celebration of feminine friendship and the particular texture of Paris.
